title: No One Is Paid to Explain It to You
author: Lead With Kelly
summary: Drawing on two decades inside boardrooms and deal tables, the author argues that most consequential systems, from corporate power structures to mortgage contracts, run on an unwritten 'real layer' that no one is incentivized to explain to outsiders, because clarity would erase the advantage insiders hold. The piece generalizes from workplace politics (decisions made in hallways before the official meeting) to the higher-stakes example of mortgage signings, citing a LoanLogics finding that more than one in nine loan files contained missing or incorrect content, costing borrowers $7.8 billion. It concludes that because explanation will never be handed to you, the only path is to keep asking questions until something actually makes sense, and to bring in experts rather than pretend to understand what you don't.
points: Argues every consequential system has two layers: an official one handed out for free, and a real, unwritten one that determines outcomes.
Uses boardroom decision-making (decisions made before the meeting, not in it) as the low-stakes version of this dynamic.
Cites a LoanLogics finding of errors in more than 1-in-9 mortgage files, costing borrowers $7.8 billion, as the high-stakes version.
Recommends refusing to sign anything you can't explain back to yourself and bringing in outside expertise rather than pretending to understand.
quotes: No one in the room is paid to remove it. And sometimes your confusion is the most profitable thing in the room.
The decisions I thought we were about to make had already been made, somewhere I was not, before the meeting was ever on the calendar. A hallway. A phone call between two people who mattered.
Reviewing a decade of files, the analytics firm LoanLogics found more than one in nine had missing or incorrect content, at a cost to borrowers of $7.8 billion.
I stopped signing anything I could not explain back to myself. And when I reached the edge of what I actually knew, I brought in an expert instead of pretending I could cover the gap myself.
Because having the information was never the same as understanding it.
